newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada premiers portray unified front at meeting.
newsitem.headline: Canada premiers portray unified front at meeting.

text.p: Canada's provincial premiers launched their annual meeting Thursday by skirting the issue of national unity and pressing federal officials to share the bounty of the recovering economy.

The premiers said they want the nation's health care system to get top priority as the need to reduce the deficit eases, but left open the question of whether that would come at the expense of income tax cuts.

The leaders, holding their 38th annual meeting, said there was no discussion of national unity, which was at the center of a political spat Wednesday between New Brunswick Premier Frank McKenna and pro-separatist Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard.
McKenna, who is hosting the meeting at a seaside resort hotel, sought Thursday to downplay the dispute over a letter of support he wrote to an anti-separatist group in Quebec.
Bouchard denounced the letter, which was made public on the eve of the gathering.

"Every (premiers') conference I've come to we have an opening ritualistic tossing of the grenade, and everything gets interesting and then we sit down, roll up our sleeves and we do business," McKenna told reporters.

The premiers emerged from their initial meetings focusing on areas where they agreed to work together, including "strengthening" the equalization formula used to distribute federal assistance to the provinces.

"Large provinces agreed that the equalization formula should work to the benefit of all Canadians, and there was a clear acknowledgement that some parts of Canada are not recovering as quickly as other parts," said McKenna.

He added that while premiers were still dedicated to fiscal discipline on both the provincial and federal level but as funds become available, they wanted investment in the country's health care system.

"A very clear consensus emerged that the most important issue facing Canadians was health care," McKenna said, predicting Canada would soon see the "fruits" of deficit fighting and an improved economy.
In addition, the provincial leaders said they would push the federal government for a cut in unemployment insurance payments once the federal budget is balanced.
The conference continues through Friday. Just how long the premiers would be able to avoid another public fight over Quebec's future in Canada remained to be seen.

The formal agenda for gathering reflected Bouchard's demand that the premiers not discuss national unity during the meeting. But at least one of the leaders acknowledged he was unhappy with that decision.
"I don't intend to take a position where you can't talk about it because Premier Bouchard is here and you can't talk about it because he is not here," said Saskatchewan Premier Roy Romanov.
Regional differences could also flare over a proposal by the premiers of economically powerful Ontario and Alberta for more provincial control over federal social programs.
